items.fullDescription: Call for Papers From its inception, cinema has transcended borders through the movement of people, capital, narratives, and visual technology. However, over the past two decades, the term transnational cinema has evolved into one of the most influential and contested frameworks in film studies. Scholars such as Elizabeth Ezra, Terry Rowden, Deborah Shaw, Will Higbee, and Song Hwee Lim have variously expanded, critiqued, and redefined the concept, emphasizing its aesthetic, political, and industrial dimensions and prompting new questions about its theoretical and pedagogical implications. While these approaches have illuminated the circulation of films, filmmakers, and spectators across borders, they have also raised questions about the continuing relevance of the national cinema framework and the analytical boundaries of the transnational itself. This symposium revisits the concept of transnational cinema at a moment when two distinct currents seem bound for collision. On the one hand, global migration, digital media, the global climate catastrophe, geopolitical conflicts, and transregional collaborations have blurred distinctions between the local and the global, as well as the national and the transnational. On the other hand, isolationism, authoritarianism, and protectionism have re-erected physical and ideological borders across the globe. Is the world more or less transnational as a result of these competing impulses? We invite proposals that address theoretical, historical, or pedagogical questions, such as: How can the familiar concept of transnational cinema elucidate emergent and unfamiliar problems in the contemporary landscape? How do we define and teach transnational cinema now? Is transnational cinema best understood as a framework, an approach, a mode of filmmaking, or a category of world cinema? How does transnational cinema intersect with, or diverge from, national, world, and global cinema theories? What are the political, aesthetic, or ethical stakes of emphasizing transnationality in film studies today? We welcome both theoretical interventions and case studies from diverse regions and traditions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: • Theories and definitions of transnational cinema • Pedagogical approaches to transnational cinema • Feminist, queer, and trans approaches to transnational cinema • Transnational authorship and stardom • Memory, trauma, and postmemory in transnational film • Digital technologies and virtual transnational spaces • Streaming platforms and global distribution • Cinemas of diaspora, exile, and migration • Cross-border activism and solidarity through film • Environmental and ecological transnationalism • Film policy, censorship, and cultural diplomacy • Transnational labor, precarity, and creative economies • International film festivals and global circulation • Archival and historiographical approaches to transnational film • Politics of translation, dubbing, and subtitling • Regional and transregional filmmaking practices • Anti-colonial, postcolonial, and de-colonial aesthetics and narratives • Global Hollywood and transnational co-productions• Transnational spectatorship and global audiences • State, statelessness, and belonging in transnational cinema • Borders, border-crossings, and redefinitions of home • Transnational genres • De-Westernizing film studies Presenters will be invited to submit completed papers for consideration in an edited collection or special issue developed from the symposium. Proposals (250-300 words) and short bios (100 words) should be submitted by June 1st, 2026, using this Google Form: https://forms.gle/R7Jw98KpMEc7BAHo6 For questions, please contact the organizing committee at ahtfilmstudies@utdallas.edu.

items.fullDescription: Tentative Title- Beyond the Ocean: Maritime Infrastructure and Hydro-Narratives of Indians under the Raj Concept Note The imperial ships of the British Raj bore millions of Indian migrants across waterways just the way Charon ferried souls across the river Styx to an irreversible fate. Nonetheless, the Indians transformed the vicious vessels into spaces of radical rebirth and enduring kinship. While the first volume in this series geographically mapped the global representations of Indian migration under the British Empire, Volume 2 moves into a critical interrogation of colonial history through ports, maritime framework, and waterways. Moving away from land-bound histories, this volume initiates an intensive interrogation of colonial history through its maritime infrastructures: ports, dockyards, maritime records, and waterways. This book adopts a hydrocolonial and aqua-centric hermeneutic to explore how subaltern narratives were historically erased from official imperial records, shipping registers, and mainstream historiography. It will examine the ports, vessels, inland rivers, and vast oceans that witnessed the diverse, turbulent flows of Indian populations across the globe. We invite chapter proposals that explore how literary depictions illustrate the ways the British Empire transformed global waterways into networks of imperial power, capital, and radical identity transformation. The psychological and structural undoing of native culture began long before the ship reached the open ocean. In the liminal, high-stress spaces of the colonial dockyards and ports, social hierarchies began to collapse. Diaspora literature, folk traditions, travelogues, and ship logs frequently evoke the immediate and profound breakdown of caste and religious boundaries the moment emigrants set foot on the regimented ports. Sudden intermixing occurred in these crowded transit camps as we witnessed Brahmins consuming food prepared by lower-caste hands, Hindus and Muslims shared sleeping quarters, and sacred visual markers of identity (turbans, sacred threads, prayer beads, religious caps, and tilaks) were stripped or voluntarily discarded to avoid surveillance, standing out, or segregation upon reaching destination ports. Once aboard, the ship itself became a volatile micro-world, sort of floating world suspended between an old life and an uncertain future. Significantly, many post-slavery labour migrations repurposed slave ships to transport new, freer workforce alongside other cargo. Textual representations from this middle passage vividly capture the horrors of overcrowding, disease, and racial prejudice. Yet, the vessel can be read as a site of profound subaltern resilience. Indian migrants forged deep, enduring bonds that acted as vital substitutes for the blood relations left behind, helping them survive the culture shock and grief of displacement. The songs, stories, and archives of this passage are filled with narratives of maritime resistance, shipboard revolts, and haunting tragedies that demand our critical attention. Book II of the Beyond the Ocean series invites proposals that capture the Indian migrant experience from port to port during the British Raj. Echoing Kamau Brathwaite's conceptualization of the tidal experience, we welcome essays that explore the large-scale, long-term dispersion of Indians across the global maritime network, starting from the Gulf nations and the African continent to Southeast Asia, American states, and the archipelagic Caribbean islands. Suggested areas for submission, including, but not limited to: Literary depictions of port architecture, custom houses, dockyards, and the initial dismantling of caste/religious identities. Ship as a total institution, the legacy of repurposed slave ships, and narratives of disease, discipline, and imperial surveillance at sea. Textual and musical representations of shipboard kinship, solidarity, and emotional survival among diverse migrant groups. Songs, oral histories, and literary accounts of maritime mutinies, escapes, sabotage, and shipboard tragedies. How the crossing of the Kala Pani (black waters) fractured and reshaped languages, creating creolized idioms, plantation songs, and hybrid oral traditions. Comparative literary readings of different aquatic journeys- including indentured labourers, penal convicts, Lascar sailors, Kangani System, Maistry System, Sepoys, and Colonial Constabularies, and free passage merchants. Literary representation of Indian ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and other water bodies. Literary representation of ship and its infrastructure. Literary representation of the ocean as repository of forgotten/suppressed history and marginalized culture. Comparative study of the Middle Passage and the Kala Pani crossing or other hydro-crossings and its literary representation. Abstract submission deadline: 31st July 2026 Word limit: 250- 350 words with 4-5 keywords Submissions in a word document along with a brief bio-note to be sent to: shubhankukochar@outlook.com You can find Book I (Beyond the Ocean: Literature, History and the British Empire) via this link https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-95-2137-1. Note: As Book I was published by Springer, the editors have submitted the proposal for Book II to Springer as well, aiming to establish this as a long-running series. Editors: Dr. Shubhanku Kochar (Associate Professor, University School of Humanities and Social Sciences at Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, Delhi) Dr. Shehnaz Kabir (Research and Development Officer, Loreto College, Kolkata)

items.fullDescription: About the Organiser Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies (DILS), Durgapur, West Bengal, is an institution dedicated to legal education and professional training. The Institute is affiliated with Kazi Nazrul University and approved by the Bar Council of India. DILS offers 5-year B.A. LL.B. (Hons.) and 3-year LL.B. (Hons.) programmes and seeks to integrate doctrinal legal education with practical exposure, research, critical thinking, and professional development. The seminar is being organised by Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies (DILS) in collaboration with its Research & Development Committee, as an IQAC Initiative. About the Seminar Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies is organising a National Level Seminar titled: "Questing the Horizon of International Law and New World Order: Jurisprudential Aspects, Contemporary Challenges, and Emerging Perspectives" The contemporary global order is witnessing significant transformation due to shifting geopolitical dynamics, evolving governance structures, technological developments, and emerging legal challenges. Against this background, the seminar seeks to explore the changing horizons of legal systems at both international and domestic levels. The seminar aims to provide a platform for academicians, practitioners, researchers, professionals, and students to engage in meaningful academic deliberations on jurisprudential developments, contemporary challenges, and emerging perspectives concerning law and governance. The seminar will be conducted in Hybrid Mode, enabling both physical and virtual participation. items.fullDescription: Abstract: This panel reexamines life writing in the age of Generative AI, asking who controls the conditions under which individuals narrate their own lives. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for authorship, equity, and cultural power, are especially welcome. Full CFP: Generative AI has fundamentally changed how we think, articulate, and write. However, access to AI is not equitable, and its outputs frequently fail to account for diverse lived experiences and reflect biases. The corporations developing AI models are agents actively reshaping how we perceive, think, interpret, and articulate our identities and experiences. This panel examines what that means for Life Writing - defined broadly to include textual, digital, and visual formats - where individuals reflect, narrativize, and present their lived experiences in public-facing contexts. Submissions engaging the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," are especially welcome. The panel welcomes submissions that explore (but are not limited to): a) Questions of authorship for AI-assisted/AI-mediated life writings b) The aesthetics and formal transformations in the practice of Life Writing in the age of Generative AI c) Life Writings produced by or attributed to Generative AI models d) The 'Author' Persona in AI-generated/AI-mediated Life Writing e) Autoethnographic explorations of writing life with AI f) Reader/Audience response to AI-mediated/AI-generated life writings g) Questions of ethics, trust, and safety, when narrating life with AI h) Impacts of AI-mediated life writing on individuals from vulnerable and marginalized communities, diverse gender identities, racial, and cultural communities i) "Permanent Memory" of AI models and archival of individual identities j) Translation, multilingualism, and cultural limitations of Generative AI in supporting Life Writing activities Note: > Please submit your proposals only via the link: https://pamla.ballastacademic. com/Home/S/20174 > Extended Deadline to submit proposals is June 30, 2026 ; early submissions are encouraged. > The 2026 PAMLA Conference is entirely in person , in Seattle, WA, with no provision for virtual or hybrid presentations . > Please check the PAMLA website for dates and additional information

items.fullDescription: Italian Teaching Symposium 2026 - II edition "Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching" September 25-26, 2026 St. Jerome's University (University of Waterloo) & online Inspired by the theme chosen for the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, "Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l'italiano", we are pleased to announce the second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, once again endorsed by the Canadian Association for Italian Studies (CAIS). Building on the success of its inaugural 2025 edition, which welcomed more than fifty participants - including presenters, chairs, and attendees from both academia and cultural institutions - this year's symposium will take place on September 25-26, 2026, at St. Jerome's University, federated with the University of Waterloo (Ontario, Canada). While primarily designed as an in-person event, limited opportunities for remote participation may be available. The second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching, aims to bring together scholars, researchers, language educators, teacher trainers, graduate students, and practitioners interested in exploring three interconnected dimensions of Italian language education: imagine, design, and create. As Marcel Danesi (2025) observes, "the study of creativity crosses all disciplinary boundaries", making creativity a particularly productive lens through which to examine the teaching and learning of Italian language and culture. This resonates well with the theme of the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, inspired by the newly established Directorate General for Growth and Export Promotion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which highlights the creative potential of Italian as a language capable of fostering ideas, innovation, and intercultural dialogue. In this sense, teaching Italian extends beyond the transmission of grammar and pronunciation to encompass cultural mediation, collaboration, and engagement with diverse forms of expression. In this context, we invite proposals that reflect on how this perspective inspires - or challenges - instructors to adopt creative and unconventional approaches to course design, including content, activities, teaching methods, and assessment. In addition to traditional paper presentations, the 2026 edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium will introduce a new hands-on session format designed to foster practical exchange, experimentation, and collaborative learning. These interactive sessions will give participants the opportunity to showcase classroom activities, digital tools and apps, pedagogical resources, multimodal projects, creative assignments, community-engaged initiatives, assessment tools, or other innovative practices implemented in Italian language and culture courses. This format is intended to encourage active engagement and discussion, allowing attendees to learn directly from colleagues' experiences and to leave the symposium with practical ideas and materials that can be adapted to their own teaching contexts. items.fullDescription: The sea and marine life are often considered as pillars of cultural heritage, identity, and collective memories in Portugal (Lourenço 2001; Lourenço 2014). From the historical milestones of the sixteenth century transoceanic navigation (Cortesão 1978) to literary production (Avelar 2024), the ocean has shaped the national imagination of Portugal (Tomás 2013). As Antonio Barreto writes: "Heritage is a human creation and the results from history and culture. But there are natural realities that are transformed, through history, culture, and technology into heritage. Such is the case of the sea for the Portuguese" (2019: 15). As a form of heritage, this connection extends to gastronomy and, in a particularly profound way, to the musical sphere (Simões 2013: 45-62; Sardo 2013: 44-64). From fado, with its narratives of longing and loss, to the songs that gave rhythm to the the fishermen's daily work, the Portuguese musical repertoire has functioned as a living archive of human interaction with the environment. However, there is nothing natural or essentialist about this Portuguese relationship with the sea, for it is an imaginary that has been constructed and continously negotiated across historical periods, which also bears the imprint of colonialism (João 2015: 119-147; El-Shawan Castelo-Branco et al 2003: 73-142). More dramatically, the transformations driven by climate change and unsustainable industrial fishing in the twenty-first century threaten not only biodiversity (Ramos-Pereira 2004: 26-43), but also the cultural practices linked to it - a topic that still requires greater attention in schoarly research. In any case, beyond its material and economic dimensions, the sea in Portugal remains a space of imagination and transformation. As evoked in the songs of José Afonso, the sea is not just a site of identity and homecoming, but also a place of alterity and utopia. By singing of the sea, we evoke the possibility of a new era, in which culture and nature meet once again in a shared project of humanity - a vision that also resonates with the notion of the Blue Humanities (Mentz 2023; Oppermann 2019: 443-461). This call seeks to explore the intersection between what we have inherited and what we must protect. Therefore, we invite researchers, artists, and cultural practitioners to reflect on how these environmental changes reshape the meaning of the arts and their role as vehicles of identity and resistance. Papers are welcome on the following topics, amongst others: The sea as a cultural construct in Portuguese music and the arts; Music, critique, and resistance to climate crises in Portugal; Intersections between literature, music, and environmental heritage; Representations of the sea and music in literature and written culture; Music, sound, identity, and the politics of ocean memory; Collective memory, local identities, and soundscapes; The sea in film, the media, and popular culture; Folklore, folk groups, and the preservation of intangible cultural heritage; Coloniality and decoloniality of contemporary maritime identity; Transcultural and postcolonial perspectives on the maritime imaginary; Blue Humanities and music as an environmental archive; Resistance, utopia, and sound activism in the face of climate change; Tourism and heritage preservation of coastal musical cultures; Technology, marine sciences, and music; Ocean ethics, music, and maritime imaginaries; Phenomenology, aesthetics, listening, and maritime experience. Contributions may be in Portuguese or English. items.fullDescription: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics include, but are not limited to, autoethnography, digital self-representation, intersectional approaches to life writing, and the emerging impacts of technological shifts-such as generative AI-on authorship and equity. Desctription : How do we articulate, preserve, and present our lived experiences in an era marked by rapid cultural and technological change? Aligning with the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," this roundtable invites participants to investigate the shifting landscape of life writing across textual, digital, and visual formats. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Examples of subtopics by discipline: Cultural Studies : analyzing representations of ecological and linguistic wastelands - including their recuperation and adaptation - in media and literature of former and current power sites and/or in post/neocolonial texts. Linguistics : examining how ecological loss accelerates language endangerment or, conversely, how language erosion facilitates ecological loss; reflecting on whether documentation practices themselves risk reproducing extractive models Sociolinguistics : studies of language contact in climate-displaced communities; examining codeswitching as ecological adaptation Translation Studies : translating environmental knowledge across Indigenous and minoritized languages without epistemic extraction Pedagogy : designing care-centred, place-based curricula that link environmental justice with multilingual education Communication Studies : analyzing how environmental crises and linguistic marginalization are framed across media, policy discourse, and digital platforms; probing how choice of language used in the media influences how communities think about ecological issues and/or manufactures consent Second-Language Teaching : incorporating local ecological narratives into L2 classrooms to foster environmental and intercultural care Minority-Language Advocacy : examining how environmental policy, urban planning, and disaster response frequently neglect linguistic accessibility, thereby compounding abandonment or proposing strategies for integrating language justice into climate-resilience planning Those interested in contributing to the conference with a 20-minute paper should send a title, 200-word abstract, and short biography to crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca by June 15, 2026. Colloque international Résister à l'abandon: langue, culture et écologie Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures Collège universitaire Glendon, Université York (Toronto, Canada) 15 et 16 octobre 2026 Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les manières dont l'écologie interagit avec le contact entre les langues, avec les transformations culturelles et avec les pratiques pédagogiques. Résister à l'abandon s'inspire de l'ouvrage marquant de Sunaura Taylor, Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), qui remet en question les récits environnementaux dominants à la lumière du handicap, du respect et de l'interdépendance. Le colloque vise à approfondir la théorisation de l'abandon, à la fois matériel et idéologique, proposée par Taylor, qui se manifeste dans des paysages pollués, des communautés dépossédées, des langues en voie de disparition et des corps marginalisés. La dégradation écologique et l'érosion linguistique évoluent souvent conjointement, façonnées par le colonialisme, l'extractivisme, les migrations et les restructurations néolibérales. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. Les menaces qui pèsent sur la diversité linguistique peuvent ainsi être reliées à l'appauvrissement de la biodiversité. Résister à l'abandon mettra en avant l'idée que les langues, à l'instar des écosystèmes, constituent des espaces de relation et de respect. Lorsque des communautés sont déplacées par des crises climatiques, la dépossession économique ou d'autres facteurs, leurs pratiques linguistiques se transforment, s'hybrident ou risquent de disparaître. Pourtant, les zones de contact engendrent également des formes créatives de survie: de nouveaux vernaculaires, des savoirs incarnés et des solidarités au-delà des différences. Le colloque réunit des chercheur·e·s, enseignant·e·s, traducteurs/trices, artistes et militant·e·s communautaires afin d'examiner comment les pratiques de nomination, de narration, d'enseignement et de traduction peuvent résister à l'abandon écologique, linguistique et culturel. Comment les métaphores de pureté et de contamination influencent-elles les politiques environnementales et linguistiques? Que peut nous apprendre la justice du handicap sur le maintien d'écologies multilingues accessibles? De quelle manière la traduction peut-elle fonctionner comme une forme de soin environnemental? Les participant·e·s réfléchiront aux enjeux éthiques et politiques liés à l'attention portée aux écologies fragiles, humaines et plus qu'humaines, sans reproduire des récits de perte qui justifient davantage de négligence. Résister à l'abandon invite à une réflexion collective sur le respect en tant que méthode, sur le contact comme créativité et sur l'interdépendance comme cadre pour penser les futurs écologiques et linguistiques. Exemples de sous-thèmes par discipline : Études culturelles : analyser les représentations des déserts écologiques et linguistiques, y compris leur récupération et leur adaptation, dans les médias et la littérature issus de centres de pouvoir, anciens ou actuels, et/ou dans des textes post/néocoloniaux Linguistique : examiner comment la perte écologique accélère la disparition des langues ou, inversement, comment l'érosion linguistique facilite la perte écologique; réfléchir à la possibilité que les pratiques de documentation elles-mêmes reproduisent des modèles extractivistes Sociolinguistique : étudier le contact entre les langues dans des communautés déplacées par les changements climatiques; analyser l'alternance codique comme forme d'adaptation écologique Traductologie : traduire les connaissances environnementales dans les langues autochtones et minoritaires sans extraction épistémique Pédagogie et didactique : concevoir des programmes axés sur les soins et ancrés dans le territoire, qui associent la justice environnementale à l'éducation multilingue Études en communication : analyser la manière dont les crises environnementales et la marginalisation linguistique sont représentées dans les médias, les discours politiques et les plateformes numériques; examiner comment les choix linguistiques dans les médias influencent la manière dont les communautés pensent les enjeux écologiques et contribuent à fabriquer le consentement Enseignement d'une langue seconde : intégrer des récits écologiques locaux dans les cours de langue seconde afin de promouvoir le respect de l'environnement et l'ouverture interculturelle Promotion des langues minoritaires : examiner comment les politiques environnementales, l'urbanisme et les interventions en cas de catastrophe négligent souvent l'accessibilité linguistique, ce qui accentue l'abandon de ces communautés, ou proposer des stratégies visant à intégrer la justice linguistique dans la planification de la résilience climatique Si vous souhaitez contribuer au colloque avec une communication de 20 minutes, veuillez envoyer un titre, un résumé de 200 mots et une courte biographie à crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca avant le 15 juin 2026. items.fullDescription: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the exception but the rule," as Walter Benjamin theorized. It is not a single event but what Lauren Berlant called a norm "embedded" in the everyday. In the zones of crisis and in daily life, the emergency overwhelms the senses, requiring constant self-governance and limiting our political imagination. The urgent threat of climate change, though often disavowed, is at the center of today's general atmosphere of crisis. Walls hold back displaced populations and rising seas. Earth systems sustain lasting damage. Species are devastated. And with apocalyptic alacrity, capitalist-imperialist competition crosses terrains that were once uninviting and hostile, from deserts to the polar regions and outer space. So far, discourses of risk and emergency have mostly been a boon for the racist right and anti-democratic technocrats, rather than contributing to a genuine project of planetary stewardship. The quest for "energy sovereignty" has unleashed a wave of extractive interventions in the Global South amid the collapse of the postwar international order, creating new sacrifice zones and colonial resource frontiers. Amid widespread doubts about electoral institutions' ability to deliver systemic transformation, some environmentalists have even embraced climate doomerism or the technosolutionism of geoengineering. We see how climate crisis is increasingly governed through biopolitical management, securitized borders, and technocratic forms of environmental control-and how the emergency becomes yet another opportunity for further administration. Crisis discourse often privileges spectacular catastrophe while obscuring the slow, uneven, and racialized forms of ecological violence embedded in everyday life. Unlike the "fevered immediacy that governs the society of the catastrophe-as-spectacle," as Rob Nixon writes, unspectacular "slow violence" is dispersed over time. With the sirens blaring, it is easy to lose sight of the material impacts of the ideology of crisis across time and space. We can also miss the ways in which the permanent emergency warps our cultural production and social relations, concealing the most pressing contradictions of capitalism today. How might we map the cartography of crisis? In doing so, might we open space for alternative ways of thinking and living within and against crisis? How do we hold crisis at bay long enough to bring about a "real state of emergency," as Benjamin says is our task? Jason W. Through this cartography of crisis, we hope to understand how we might countermap and counteract this state of ecological and social emergency. We invite proposals from graduate students in the humanities and social sciences, as well as artists, writers, and other practitioners. Our goal is to create space for imagination and speculation with people of varied backgrounds, interests, and praxes. We welcome interdisciplinary scholarship and cultural criticism attentive to the cultural, aesthetic, historical, and political dimensions of crisis. items.fullDescription: Call for Contributors Into the Fog: Essays on Dead by Daylight The call for papers has been extended to August 21st, 2026. While we are particularly interested in submissions dealing with lore and worldbuilding, survival horror, fandom, online discourse, anime and horror, and transmedia ventures and shared worlds of horror, we welcome all topics. Dead by Daylight (DBD) is an asymmetric four versus one online horror game where a team of survivors must work together to escape from a brutal killer, developed and published by Behavior Interactive. From its debut in 2016 the game has risen to become one of the most popular horror gaming experiences. As a live-service game with frequent updates, the game has developed a notable community following with prominent streamers, content creators, and popular memes. The game has inspired fans to cosplay, stream their matches, and develop fanart and fanfiction. The game is also known for its frequent collaborations with classic and emerging horror franchises, including Halloween , Nightmare on Elm Street , Alien , Stranger Things , Five Nights at Freddy's , and drag performers The Boulet Brothers. The game has also had different versions and spinoffs including Dead By Daylight Mobile (Behavior Interactive 2020) and The Casting of Frank Stone (Supermassive Games 2024). In November 2023, the gaming site Polygon reported Dead by Daylight reached 60 million players, and the game is celebrating its tenth anniversary in 2026. We invite proposals for original, unpublished essays that explore the different facets of horror and gaming in Dead by Daylight for an edited volume under contract with McFarland. We welcome interdisciplinary submissions from all career stages, including independent scholars and graduate students. Submissions should be scholarly but accessible to a general audience. The collection will be published in English, but we welcome submissions from and are eager to work with scholars working in other languages who are interested in publishing new work on the game in English. Suggested topics with DBD may include, but are not limited to, the following: · Lore and worldbuilding · Fan culture and community · Horror in video games and the survival horror genre · Transmedia ventures and shared worlds of horror - Anime and horror · Toxicity and online discourse · World horror, folk horror, internet horror, and transnational dimensions of horror · LGBTQ+ representation and community · Race, horror, and survival · The monstrous feminine, final girls, and women in horror · Cosplay and fan work · Embodiment and avatars · Accessibility and horror games · Interfaces and game menus · Ruins, rust, and history in horror · Game mechanics, balancing updates, and fairness · Affect and abjection · Player sentiment and experiences · Licensing, collaborations, and merchandising Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 300 words, as well as brief author bios, should be submitted to Daniel Fandino (Daniel.Fandino@ucf.edu) & Cody Mejeur (codymeje@buffalo.edu) by our extended deadline of August 21, 2026 . The editors will review all submitted proposals and notify applicants by the end of August 2026. Chapters should be approximately between 5000-8000 words, and first drafts of completed manuscripts will be due December 15, 2026. The expected publication date will be 2027-2028. Note: Acceptance of a proposed abstract does not guarantee the acceptance of the full chapter. Chapters will undergo both editor and peer review. About the Editors Daniel Fandino (PhD) is the coordinator of the Digital Exploration Center at the University of Central Florida. He has previously co-edited a book on the Marvel cinematic universe for McFarland and has written articles on EVE Online and the history of computer gaming. Cody Mejeur (They/them, PhD) is Assistant Professor of Media Study at University at Buffalo, SUNY, and Director of the Amatryx Gaming Lab & Studio there. They are currently the game director for Trans Folks Walking , a narrative game about trans experiences. They are an editor of Historiographies of Game Studies (punctum 2025), co-editor of the trans narratology special issue of the Narrative journal (2024) and have published numerous articles and book chapters in Games & Culture , Digital Humanities Quarterly , and Resilience: A Journal of the Environmental Humanities , among others. items.fullDescription: "It is worse, much worse, than you think" states David Wallace-Wells at the opening of his The Uninhabitable Earth: Life After Warming (2019). "When do we start physically attacking the things that consume our planet and destroy them with our own hands?" asks Andreas Malm in How to Blow Up a Pipeline (2021). "I don't think about hope much anymore. But I do think about imagination," writes Terry Tempest Williams in an interview contained in A voice in the Wilderness: Conversations with Terry Tempest Williams (2006). In the spaces between these statements we encounter a range of reactions to our warming condition, from blunt pessimism, to righteous anger, to nuanced reframing. Triangulating these sentiments, we arrive at an undeniable point of ecopessimism, an overwhelming feeling that everything is speeding toward destruction, the painful realization that perhaps Earth, "the only home we've ever known" to quote Carl Sagan, is no longer so welcoming. Counterintuitively, the narrative trope of the looming threat of an "inhospitable earth" may facilitate a denial of the reality of climate crisis. The narrative ubiquity of natural disasters, futures of scarcity, and apocalyptic hellscapes results in a figuring of an Earth incompatible with human life as an easily dispelled bogeyman looming familiarly, and therefore toothlessly, over future climate scenarios. What happens, however, if we read the "end of the world" instead as an ego death of the anthropocene? If the idea of an "inhospitable earth" no longer gains imaginative traction in advocacy or art, then we are tasked with imagining an afterlife for Earth as informed by an ethic of hospitality. The opposite of an "inhospitable earth" is not merely one that is conducive to human survival; being "hospitable" is defined as "affording welcome and entertainment to strangers." How can an ethic of hospitality bend ecopessimism into something worth, as it were, entertaining? If the "end of the world" is certain, what might it look like, as Wendell Berry poetically urges us, to "practice resurrection"? This ASLE affiliated panel welcomes proposals that address the question of how to live (and entertain) in a world on fire. We are especially interested in work that moves beyond abstract hope and optimism to address the complex and overwhelming force of the overlapping crises of our time. If the worst must be assumed, where does that leave us? And what imaginings should we entertain while here? Possible topics may include: -The roles and limits of art and literature in addressing world crises. -Climate realism, doomerism, ecofascism, abundance and other ideologies that address the realities of an inhospitable Earth. -The uses/abuses of hope in understanding and planning for possible inhospitable futures. -The place of imagination in creating more hospitable futures. -Successes/Failures of environmental/climate justice in creating more equitable futures. -The image of technology such as A.I. or space travel as solutions to or escapes from climate collapse. -Treatment of the Other, broadly conceived, in light of environmental/climate crisis. -Any other topic that considers the overbearing presence of climate collapse, open subject area and time period. Please send abstracts of 250-500 words, along with A/V requirements and a brief bio, to Jency Wilson (jwilson17@una.edu) and Matt Spencer (mls0142@auburn.edu) by 24 August 2026.

items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). Papers in STEM fields that clearly articulate relevance to the theme are welcome. Full-panel proposals will be given priority. Panel proposals must include a 200-250 word proposal for the panel in addition to abstracts for each individual participant. A select number of travel grants will be awarded on a competitive basis for those traveling more than 100 miles. To qualify for a travel grant, you must submit your application by August 14, 2026. Further details will be included in your registration sign-up. Please submit abstracts via the following google form link: https://tinyurl.com/2026ERAH

This session will convene scholars and practitioners to collaboratively explore best practices for teaching museum ethics across a range of educational contexts. Contributors are encouraged to share case studies, assignments, classroom strategies, or institutional partnerships and reflective assessments of successes and tensions encountered in teaching ethical issues. items.fullDescription: Overall Conference Theme of the 7th Edition Tourism has never seen the development of artificial intelligence (AI) as fast as we see today. This includes the automation of tourist interaction, use of predictive analytics for their data, and increasing use of personalized systems with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI) that can produce all sorts of content from texts, images, travel itineraries, and even support tourist decision-making processes. An "AI turn" in tourism is now becoming increasingly common with many observers referring to a moment similar to previous digital or platform turn. However, there is one question remaining: Does this shift toward AI truly represent a structural transformation of the industry, or is it simply a change in rhetoric that redefines the way we approach innovation? There has been a growing body of academic research examining how artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into tourists' practices and experiences. However, there remains a limited understanding of the depth and extent of the transformation that AI may bring to the tourism sector. While AI clearly illustrates evolving changes in service delivery and customer interactions-particularly through tools such as large language models like ChatGPT-its applications extend further. AI is now being used for trip planning, customer communication, and the creation of marketing content, among other functions, thereby enhancing and, in some cases, automating service delivery. According to Sigala (2024), the use of generative AI (GenAI) will continue to shape how customers interact with tourism and hospitality products, by transforming value co-creation processes and redefining customer engagement with businesses. Additionally, Bulchand-Gidumal et al. (2024) suggest that AI could significantly alter tourism marketing practices, particularly through hyper-personalization, predictive targeting, and automation. Nevertheless, these emerging applications also pose important challenges for companies, especially in balancing the appropriate level of human involvement with machine-driven interactions in service encounters. On the other hand, many reviews of late have cautioned against associating technological adoption with structural change. In an integrated review of generative AI in tourism management, Li (2025) observes that a great deal of empirical research between 2022 and 2024 has focused on applications and functionalities of generative AI instead of actual organization-wide change. Therefore, the literature remains conceptually fragmented, and robust theoretical frameworks explaining how AI produces sustained managerial change are still emerging. Fouad, Salem, and Fathy (2024) similarly observe that while GenAI is growing fast within tourism and hospitality research, there are also persistent concerns relating to algorithmic bias, governance, transparency, and accountability which will comprise claims of fully realized transformations. The debate becomes even more complex within smart tourism ecosystems. Koo et al. (2025), proposed an "AI-powered smart tourism 2.0" model with the aim of redefining how destinations are governed and resources can be allocated and decisions made in real time by destination management organizations. These changes however appear to have an unevenness and reliance upon several factors including digital maturity, institutional capability and strategic alignment. For these reasons, Buhalis et al. (2024) argue that the adoption of technology in tourism is often incremental, rather than an abrupt change in management. Therefore, it is possible that the AI turn will merely be another form of reinforcing existing structures rather than challenging them. Beyond the efficiency of the operation of AI, it is important to analyze the socio- organizational implications of this technological transition. The reviews on the conversational AI show that there are benefits in terms of increased efficiency and customer satisfaction, yet they also highlight the need for trust, acceptance, and the ethical protections necessary for the use of this technology. In addition, at a policy level, the OECD (2024) has highlighted concerns with respect to the reorganization of work, the need for the reconfiguration of skills, privacy issues, and the need to adapt regulations. Depending on the actions taken by governments, these factors can either accelerate or limit the extent of the transformation associated with the adoption of AI. Overall, this body of research clearly demonstrates that AI has changed both service design and operational practices for tourism. Whereas, it is an empirical and theoretical matter as to whether the "AI turn" will result in the transformation of governance structures, organizational architectures, the professional roles of people working in the industry, and the strategic decisions made by them. As such, the conference theme invites submissions from researchers that provide critical assessments of what is being done with AI in tourism today and whether there is a new form of substantive change in the way the industry is operated, or simply a new form of a powerful narrative about technology. Multidisciplinary perspectives-including management, economics, sociology, geography, anthropology, law, and information systems-are strongly encouraged. items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: SAMLA Conference November 5-7, 2026, Atlanta CFP: Teaching Migrations and Diaspora in Language and Content Classrooms (Roundtable) Teaching classes on migration and diaspora can be both very rewarding and challenging. Whether it's a literature, documentary, and/or cinema class that focuses on migration, or an activity designed to introduce these topics in language classes at all levels, instructors must be able to navigate difficult conversations, making sure that the discussion remains productive and inclusive even when it creates discomfort. In line with this year's theme of "Hospitality", this roundtable invites short (5- 10-minute) presentations that explore ideas and content related to migrations and diaspora in any language and content classes. What texts do we include in our syllabi to address both hospitality and, more often, inhospitality towards migrants and refugees? What in-class activities, homework, and assessments do we design to elicit students' reflections on such complicated themes? In terms of teaching strategies, which ones can we use to make sure all students feel included in class and in the conversation? What decolonial practices can we utilize to foster both a positive class environment and impactful discussions? Can AI help us with any of these tasks? Presentations may focus on cultural production and primary sources used in L2/LS and content classes related to any languages, migrant communities, or diasporic cultures (including, but not limited to, Afro-Italian, Afro-Brazilian, Italian-American, Asian-American, internal migrations) or on pedagogical aspects, activities, and practices. Please submit a 200- 250-word abstract and a short bio through the SAMLA website by September 1, 2026 (https://samla. ballastacademic.com/Home/S/ 19672). For questions, don't hesitate to contact the roundtable organizers: Giuseppina Gemboni (ggemboni@andrew.cmu.edu) and Francisco (Paco) Chen-López (paco@spelman.edu).

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. Editors: Cristina Santos Pinheiro, Joaquim Pinheiro, Rui Carlos Fonseca, Samuel Mateus, Telmo Reis e Vanessa Cesário Proposals, in Word format, should be submitted by 10 September 2026 to the following email address: retorica.comunicacao@mail.uma.pt The Volume is scheduled for publication in March 2027 by a leading national publisher. All submissions will be subject to scientific evaluation (blind peer review). Authors will be notified of the review decision by 30 November 2026. 1. Accepted languages Submissions will be accepted in Portuguese, French, English, and Spanish. 2. Formatting guidelines 2.1. Quotations longer than three lines must be indented 1 cm from the left margin. 3.3. a) Italics should be used for the titles of works, modern monographs, and journals. b) Quotation marks (" ") should be used for quotations from modern texts. c) Italics should not be used for Latin abbreviations (op. cit., loc. cit., cf., ibid., in…). 4. Images must be submitted in .jpeg format, with a minimum resolution of 300 dpi, be free of copyright fees, and accompanied by official proof of permission or purchase of rights for academic publication. Each submission may include no more than four images (printing will not be in color). 6. Final bibliography The bibliography should be limited to essential works or cited references and must conform to APA style (7th ed.). 7. Copyright statement Submissions must be original, and authors grant publication rights upon acceptance.

items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.excerpt: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories.
