items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. We want to make this symposium as accessible as possible; we will be working to ensure a relaxed academic environment and we encourage anyone attending to email us with any access needs. Bursaries will be available from BAAS on a limited basis for students requiring financial support for attendance. The deadline for submissions is? 15th September 2026 .?Please send proposals including a title, an abstract of no more than? 250 words ?and?a short biography of no more than 200 words ?to Claire Watt at?claire.watt@baas.ac.uk. If you have any questions about the symposium, big or small, please get in touch and we will be happy to help. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.fullDescription: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and enforcement become digitally mediated? No single discipline settles these questions. With a poster you discuss your project at the centre of the programme, alongside scholars and practitioners working on exactly these questions: Möllers (HU Berlin), Nassehi (LMU Munich), Paulus (former Justice of the German Federal Constitutional Court), Schlögl-Flierl (German Ethics Council), Foblets (MPI for Social Anthropology), Vec (University of Vienna), Hansen (State Data Protection Commissioner of Schleswig-Holstein) and Bubnys (European Commission), among others. What you get:Viisibility in front of leading scholars and practitioners rather than in a parallel session; substantive feedback in conversation plus a short written comment on your abstract; a citable peer-review process; networking with doctoral researchers from across Europe; free attendance on both days. Potential poster publication on our website. Who can apply. Doctoral researchers in law, science and technology studies, sociology, political science, philosophy and ethics, history, computer science and engineering with a societal research question, design, communication and media studies, and further or interdisciplinary fields. What matters is not your disciplinary label but your contribution to the relationship between normativity and technology. Your stage of doctorate is irrelevant: proposals, early outlines and first interim findings are as welcome as work nearing completion, and practitioners pursuing a doctorate alongside their work are invited too. From big picture to concrete cases. We welcome conceptual and foundational contributions (theories of normativity under technological change, legitimacy and the rule of law in digital governance, the interplay of legal, ethical, social and technical norms, automation of norm application, interdisciplinary methodology) as well as specific, applied and empirical work (the AI Act and data protection law in practice, platform regulation, digital administration and courts, predictive policing, health data, technical standardisation, sustainability, and case studies of individual technologies, authorities, decisions or regulatory processes). Please relate your contribution to one of the three guiding questions: (1) To what extent is technological change amenable to normative and in particular legal governance? (2) To what extent must normative orders, above all the law, themselves change? (3) What potentials and risks does the technological transformation of normativity and law entail? How it works. Each session opens with lightning talks: max. 90 seconds and one slide per poster; questions are taken at the posters rather than in the plenary. Day 1 (German, 5 November): pitch session 4:15-4:35 PM, poster session from 4:35 PM into the Apéro riche. Day 2 (English, 6 November): pitch session 11:20-11:40 AM, poster session 11:40 AM-12:35 PM before lunch. Posters are on display both days; your poster language determines your pitch day. Peer review and selection. Each anonymised abstract is assessed independently by two members of the review committee, with divergences discussed in the committee. items.fullDescription: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world literature theories, considered as an effective tool to rethink contemporary authorship issues, it encourages at the same time proposals that aim to identify and deepen conceptions of the author coming from understudied historical and geographical contexts, thereby broadening the cultural horizon of Western reflections on the subject. Indeed, we are mostly used to considering authorship as a romantic notion, strictly linked to the paradigm of genius and individuality, the authority of which was famously questioned by twentieth-century literary theory-relying primarily on such celebrated thinkers as Barthes and Foucault-before re-emerging in the post-structuralist era. However, other historical periods and cultures have not necessarily applied the same theoretical paradigms nor followed the same critical trajectory (think about collaborative or anonymous authorship in the Middle Ages, as well as the lack of the rhetoric of genius in most Far Eastern literary traditions, to give just a few non-exhaustive examples). In our opinion, it is therefore important to rethink the notion of authorship in the light of these divergent traditions, especially to ensure a more complex and multi-focal approach to it in an increasingly globalized literary context. Even though theories of world literature have profoundly transformed the ways in which the critical field of literary studies is currently understood, we argue that, in fact, the crucial category of authorship has received comparatively little sustained attention within this debate. While effectively highlighting how substantial changes in the literary system have simultaneously reconfigured the author as a global cultural agent whose visibility depends on complex networks of publishing, mediation, and institutional recognition, the world literature perspective has less frequently questioned the Western theoretical framework of authorship as a productive and individual stance. We therefore suggest that merging genealogical reflections on authorship with world literature studies could help to make the latter much more inclusive and global, rather than a mere framework of Western concepts superimposed on the literatures of the rest of the world. We welcome papers in English, French, Italian or Spanish. Possible topics include: - authorship in world literature theories; - the intersection of authorship, postcoloniality, and the global literary market; - twentieth-century theories of authorship and their global afterlives; - pre-modern, indigenous, and non-Western conceptualizations of the author; - multilingual, exilic, diasporic, and transnational authorship. Please submit your proposal through the ACLA's online paper portal by September 22, 2026 (an abstract of no more than 1,500 characters and a short bio-bibliography). Once your account has been created, simply click on the "propose a paper" button available at the following link: https://www.acla.org/ seminar/263adf13-fe6c-4fc3- 95f7-87083b14e3f9. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to contact the seminar organizers (giovanni.salvagninizanazzo@ parisnanterre.fr; federico. ristagno@phd.unict.it). Notification of acceptance will be sent by December 1, 2026.

items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? items.fullDescription: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical control, there have always been and continue to be significant moments of resistance and agency in which marginalized (colonized/Indigenous) communities have challenged or reformulated/redefined the concepts of body, disease, and health. This seminar seeks to foster a discussion in order to understand how the body can be read as a transnational figure of resistance and refusal both in the 19th century and today. Through various disciplines on the subjective and untold experiences of the body, health(care), and illness, we hope to shed light on the fluctuations in imperial medical frameworks and decolonial epistemology that pose alternative narratives-both realist and speculative-about biomedical discourses of health, gender and sexual normativity, disability/deficiency, hygiene, humanness, life/death. We are interested in questions such as: How are illnesses phrased, represented, imagined in marginalized communities? How is the effectiveness of care and therapies a scientific, ethical, and cultural problem? How can the medicalized body-or the body that is made into a site of changeability and "treatment"-become a speculative site entangling place, race, gender, and sexuality? This seminar welcomes papers that take on interdisciplinary approaches to literature and other forms of cultural production such as film, print culture, and music that engage with the theme from the 19th- 21st centuries across the world. We are especially interested in lesser-known materials and understudied communities. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: Narrative medicine from all types of media Bioethics Biopolitics and governmentality Mental health and literature, art and media studies Limitations of medical or pharmaceutical knowledge Medicalization of health/illness Marginalized bodies in medicinal knowledge (queer, disabled, racialized, female) Community/Immunity Pandemic and contagion Aging studies and end-of-life care, childcare/youth studies Utopia/Dystopia/Ecotopia Toxicity and Waste Trauma and memory studies Supernatural bodies, cyborg and alien "others", metamorphosis and transformation (Digital) post-life, afterlife studies, martyrdom Animal studies, Post-humanism To submit an abstract, please go to: https://www.acla.org/seminar/82ccd196-900f-482d-aac6-3b983a0957b2. items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.excerpt: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www....
items.fullDescription: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e Marginalised women in South Asia are read for what was done to them, far less often for what they made. This seminar asks what comparative literature can do about that. Intersectionality has become the default grammar for writing about marginalised women in the region. It arrived from a particular genealogy - Black feminist jurisprudence in the United States - into a region that had theorised compounded subordination for a century under other names: Phule on caste and women's education; Ambedkar on endogamy as the mechanism reproducing caste through control of women; Pandita Ramabai; Uma Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy; Gopal Guru's claim that Dalit women talk differently; Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint. Whether the import clarifies or flattens that inheritance is contested. Nivedita Menon argues that intersectionality serves states and donor agencies better than feminist politics; Sunaina Arya and Anandita Pan reply that the fault is citational, not conceptual. That argument has run almost entirely in social science. Our premise is that intersectionality is a diagram - a crossroads, a grid, a set of axes. Literary forms do not behave like diagrams. They work through voice, genre, meter, silence, obscenity, laughter, ritual and untranslatability. What does intersectionality look like as a reading practice rather than a taxonomy of identities? Where does form outrun the grid, and what should replace it - standpoint, assemblage, repertoire, abundance? Three provocations frame the seminar. First, the arithmetic of injury: criticism here tends to produce a tally of wounds, in which the Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim, trans, disabled or displaced woman is legible chiefly through what was done to her. Charu Gupta shows this figure has a history: in colonial Hindi reformist print the polluting "vamp" gave way to the deferential sufferer, Surpanakha displaced by Shabari, while the Dalit virangana of 1857 offered a rival image that never took. Following Gupta, Anjali Arondekar on archival abundance over loss, and Shailaja Paik on Tamasha performers who turn vulgarity into leverage, we welcome papers that read craft, expertise, pleasure and the ordinary. Second, marginality is not virtue. Tanika Sarkar's work on the Hindu wife as ground of cultural nationalism, and on women's agency inside right-wing movements, refuses to assume that subordination guarantees a critical position. We want dominant-caste women's self-writing - Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban - read alongside rather than apart from Dalit testimonio, and the complicities an axis model hides. Third, translation. Most of these texts do not exist in English. Bama's Karukku and Challapalli Swaroopa Rani's Telugu poems reach the Anglophone academy through an apparatus - glossary, preface, caste footnote, anthology - that turns literature into evidence. Swaroopa Rani's "Water" registers not only the village/wada line but the gradations within it, leather-worker and weaver. The grid has grids inside it, and translation is where they flatten. Topics might include, but are in no way limited to: the genre problem in Dalit women's testimonio; Dalit feminist poetry read as theory; the manufacture of the suffering woman in colonial print and the counter-archives that failed; nineteenth-century women's self-writing and its caste unconscious; women as agents of majoritarian politics; sung and seasonal repertoires as authorial economies rather than folklore; Adivasi women's poetry and the politics of script; landays and Afghan women's oral forms; testimonial method in Kashmir; plantation labour and memory in Sri Lanka; Muslim women and the meme as a genre of gendered communal violence; trans and hijra life-writing at the caste intersection; devadasi, Tamasha and courtesan archives read for abundance; caste in North America and Gulf labour circuits; translation as method. We invite papers on any South Asian language, region, period or diaspora. Researchers and Faculty Members at every career stage are welcome, including independent researchers and those working outside the Anglophone academy, and papers that argue against the seminar's premises are equally welcome. To submit: proposals go through the ACLA portal, not to the organisers directly. Visit https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e and use the "Propose a Paper" button. Current ACLA membership is required. Deadline 22 September 2026. We'd like to have you in person, please mention your preferred mode- ONLINE/IN PERSON along with the abstract. Enquieres: nandinigayen006@gmail.com; tamanna0602@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-human. This seminar invites scholars to discuss the monster both as a literary figure and as the representation and construction of a cultural and political identity. Through this, it aims to explore the question of where, why, and how monsters are produced, and what these monsterized creatures "show" about the communities that "produce" them. The seminar discusses how theory, from Freud's "the uncanny" to Cohen's "monster theory" to Creed's "monstrous feminine," can help us understand monsterization. The monsterized body is pushed outside the category of the "human" and thus outside the status of a rights-bearing subject. In this respect, monsterization begs the question of rights. This seminar aims to understand and make visible how the process which "produces" the Other as a monster, works in relation to rights. In Of Monsters and Migrants, Peter Arnds traces this process through Carl Schmitt's concepts of sovereignty and the "state of exception" and Agamben's biopolitics: to monsterize the migrant, the stranger, the refugee allows one to push them outside the protection of the law. As Arnds shows, the question of who - and what - monsterizes is therefore also the question of who is, or is not, recognized as a rights-bearing subject. The second focus of the seminar is the reclamation of the monster. Susan Stryker's "My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamounix" identifies the trans body with Frankenstein's creature. It reverses the accusation of the "unnatural," constructed body and transforms the words "monster" and "creature" into terms of power reclamation, self-representation, and resistance. The monster is not only a position produced by the powerful but also one that can be reclaimed by those who are monsterized. What else can we see in monsters beyond the gendered or racial Other? We encourage scholars working in different areas-literary studies, television, film and anime studies, law and human rights theory, postcolonial and critical race theory, queer and trans theory-to offer new definitions of, and reflections on, the category of the monster. We invite papers around the following questions: How does the monster negotiate who counts as "human" and who counts as a subject of human rights? What social, political, or legal aspects make a body a monster? What strategies do those who are monsterized use to reclaim their representations and rights? How do different media construct the relationship between monsters and rights? Submit your paper title and abstract through the ACLA submission portal on the ACLA website by September 22, 2026, and note that you must be logged in to see the "Propose a Paper" button. items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.fullDescription: 2027 National Advanced Writing Symposium "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing" FREE & ONLINE, Hosted by the University of Southern California Event Date: Friday, January 29, 2027 Deadline to Submit a Proposal: Friday, September 25, 2026 Link to Submit a Proposal: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd9dZiyi_mlo-G9bYPmj47EmQg07M_Xv83yap4bkd_q0i73EQ/viewform Context The USC Writing Program is delighted to host the fourth annual National Advanced Writing Symposium! The event is entirely ONLINE and FREE to both speakers and attendees, as we aim to bring together teachers of advanced and/or upper-division college composition courses to discuss innovative methods and effective practices. Our theme, "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing," welcomes participants to contemplate how Advanced Writing will address emerging needs and conditions in our discipline and beyond. Please join us and share your work in the Advanced Writing space. We hope to include a wide variety of topics, from how you theorize modes of writing beyond first-year composition to how you build your students' confidence and skills as they prepare to write in a rapidly changing, professional world beyond college. Our theme invites analyses of the multifaceted information landscapes that advanced student writers face as they transition from school writers to life writers. If selected to present at the symposium, you will also be invited to submit your work to the NAWS Online Journal , which will publish its inaugural issue in Fall 2027. Topics & Issues We welcome proposals for panels, individual presentations, workshops, and roundtables related to any of the following: The Human: How can we prioritize the humanity of knowledge production in Advanced Writing contexts? Humanist futures; innovations that embrace analog or paper-based practices; reimagining low-tech approaches; the paradox of reclaiming techniques of the past to offset the uncertainties of emerging technologies. The Generative: How is the humanity of writing in conversation with digital generative tools? Human generation versus machine synthesis; generative AI and LLMs, including contrasting views on these technologies and debates over their uses; writing as generative (because certainly, writing was generative before Chat GPT!) The Political: How can Advanced Writing pedagogies resist oppression, increase inclusion, and support social justice? The intersection of Advanced Writing and DEIB; teaching practices that fight fascism, encourage solidarity, or demonstrate "principled refusal"[1]; resisting institutional structures or social forces that estrange students from their work or each other. The Students' Futures: How might we help our students transition from "school writing" to "life writing" as they adjust to their professional worlds? Anticipating the changing needs and expectations of the professions and disciplines students are entering; professional writing; experiential learning; nonfiction genres as a form of social action.[2] The Discipline: How might Advanced Writing spaces serve to do more than rehash the rhetorical essay, but rather serve as a place to innovate pedagogies in a turbulent Higher Ed landscape? Adapting pedagogies to changing conditions; writing instructors and program administrators working in ways that are shaping or innovating our discipline; the future of Advanced Writing within the broader context of higher education. The Multifaceted Information Landscape: As a teacher or scholar of Advanced Writing, how are you playing in the multiverse? items.fullDescription: "Did I request thee, Maker?": Contemporary Cyborgs and Androids and Their Pre-Modern Antecedents Contemporary speculative fiction is saturated with androids, cyborgs, artificial intelligences, and technologically engineered forms of sentience. Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre-modern literature repeatedly imagines artificial beings, animated matter, virtual persons, mechanical servants, enchanted automata, and forms of life that blur the boundary between the human and the non-human. This panel invites papers that place contemporary representations of manufactured or technologically mediated beings in dialogue with their classical or pre-modern antecedents. Possible pairings might include science fiction, film, television, comics, anime, or video games alongside texts from antiquity through the early modern period. What conceptual, philosophical, theological, or aesthetic frameworks for artificial life emerge in pre-modern literature? How do earlier traditions of animation, embodiment, enchantment, or mechanical simulation anticipate contemporary debates surrounding AI, consciousness, labor, gender, race, affect, or personhood? While Frankenstein remains a central touchstone for discussions of artificial life-and itself invokes Paradise Lost as part of that genealogy-this panel is especially interested in less frequently discussed genealogies and archives. What ancestors to the android or cyborg might be found in Ovid's Metamorphoses, the works of Shakespeare, medieval romance, alchemical traditions, Jewish mysticism, Islamic philosophy, Buddhist narrative traditions, or other non-Western pre-modern texts? Possible topics may include automata and animated objects; artificial or manufactured bodies; alchemy, magic, and technological imagination; pre-modern theories of mind, soul, and consciousness; race, gender, and constructed embodiment; virtuality, simulation, and illusion; labor and mechanical life; monstrosity and the posthuman; game studies and worldbuilding; and theological or philosophical anxieties surrounding creation itself.

items.fullDescription: Maybe no one has ever looked at a pile of papers with unbridled joy, but in a time of university-subsidized LLMs, instructors are more likely view a stack of papers with a mix of dread and horror. How many made up quotations will I have to check? How many fake citations? How many versions of "it's not ___, it's ___" can I read before my soul leaves my body? To teach writing now is to be reminded too forcefully of the critique of writing that Plato relays in the Phaedrus: "it is no true wisdom that you offer your disciples, but only its semblance, for by telling them of many things without teaching them you will make them seem to know much, while for the most part they know nothing, and as men filled, not with wisdom but with the conceit of wisdom, they will be a burden to their fellows." Plato captures here complaints that writing teachers pestered by LLM-extruded prose should recognize immediately. Many writing teachers have responded to the creation of the semblance of wisdom and its corrosive production of conceit by turning to the solution offered in Plato: the voice. This roundtable invites participants who have shifted their pedagogy to center discussion, dialogue, oral presentation, and other forms of embodied communication in response to the depredations of LLMs in higher education. How has this use of voice affected how students write and how we think about their writing? Submit abstracts of 250 words by September 30, 2026. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. To survive, humans must extend their care and loyalty to other inhabitants of our shared planet, and co-construct knowledge -sympoeisis-with them. Haraway includes part-biological cyborgs in the potential so-called symbionts with whom humans should co-exist, but does not expressly include fully non-biologic, mechanical partners in her analysis. Yet, as part of the thought experiment enacted by speculative fictions of manufactured fellow beings, Haraway's prescription might be expanded to encompass sentient partners whom humans engineer and manufacture to keep themselves company. This roundtable invites papers interrogating speculative fiction solutions for expanding kinship relations to sentient non-biologic companions, whether embodied robots, virtual companions, or other. In other words, how does a particular creator of an imagined world envision expanding Haraway's Chthulucene era of "oddkin" to included fully artificial as well as natural companion species? And how do these artificial companions fare, that is, are the humans in their worlds able to embrace their right to equal standing and accord them rights?

items.fullDescription: Victor Hugo, Alexandre Dumas (father as well as son), William Wordsworth, Percy B. Shelley, Friedrich Hölderlin, G.W.F. Hegel… The list of writers from the era conventionally identified as "Romantic" to have become enthusiastic about the French Revolution could keep on going indefinitely. In fact, ever since the outbreak of the American Revolution in 1765, through the French and the Haitian Revolutions throughout the 1790's, all the way to 1848, the year that de-politicized Charles Baudelaire (according to his letter from May 5, 1852 to Narcisse Ancelle), literary production seems to have been inseparable from the process of building after and thinking social revolution. And that's because both Romanticism and the bourgeois upheavals of the late 18th century inherit and put to practice the Enlightened commitment to "the free, independent use of all of our predispositions and powers in thought and action," as Johann Adam Bergk put it in his 1795 article "Does Enlightenment Cause Revolutions?" But not every instance of Romanticism is revolutionary in the same way or engages with the big revolutions equally. And that's what makes the relationship so seminal. This panel invites papers that examine the relationships between literature, literary life, textual practice more broadly, and the social changes that occurred throughout the world from the mid 18th to the mid 19th century, from whichever angle and framework. While primarily focused on the influence these revolutions had on German, French, and English thought, we welcome papers dealing with other intellectual and social contexts, for as long as a clear connection between a literature that can be deemed "Romantic" and social revolutions is being drawn. Scholars from all over the world are invited. "Romanticism and Revolution" is a hybrid panel. Your presentation can be made in person or through Zoom. You are welcome to present remotely, although you can definitely take more advantage of the conference if you are there in person! This panel invites papers that discuss the relationships between literary production and revolution from the second half of the 18th century until the middle of the 19th. The discussion proposed by the paper can take any approach the author(s) find proper. While primarily focused on authors from the French, German, and English traditions, the panel welcomes papers discussing other contexts, for as long as the link between "Romanticism and Revolution" is somehow maintained. items.fullDescription: Jordan Peele's Us is a critically acclaimed horror original about government-manufactured clones that are forced to mimic the lives of the people who live on the surface like stringless puppets. While Peele focuses more on a physical tethering, there is a psychological tethering that can be gleamed from this piece, specifically as it relates to the idea of double consciousness. In his work "The Striving of the Negro People," W.E.B. Du Bois describes this idea as "this sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt or pity. One ever feels his two-ness-an American, a Negro, two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder." These "warring ideas" can exist in any group as the numerous stereotypes, prejudices, and misconceptions alive and well in the world has convinced many to fashion a Franksteined-version of themselves in the hopes of being accepted or safe. The jerky, uncoordinated movements of the tethered from the movie are the perfect metaphor for this forced reality. People attempting to push themselves to live in ways they were not meant to and should not have to. This panel is asking participants to provide submissions that explore the many ways this "tethering" has manifested in the world and explain the impact had on people's lives or how this knowledge can be used as a way to empower people and bring communities together. In other words, in what ways could we be tethered to unfair or unjust interpretations in the world and/or how could our lived experiences be used to untether us from opinions and views that do not empower us and help us build healthy communities? The chair welcomes essays, critical analysis, creative non-fiction, hybrid works, and excerpts of longer pieces.

items.fullDescription: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us-to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience "somewhere else," (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it. However, the veil is lifting, and "somewhere else" has reached us directly--worker and labor exploitation, droughts and systemic extermination of wild animals, widening class gaps, heat waves, short and snowless winters, floods, wildfires, unprecedented weather patterns, booming microbe populations that alter the very soil we stand on. A sustainable future must be an inconvenient one, and perhaps a precarious one, unless we can remake communities with a focus on outmoded forms of convenience: reciprocity, mutual aid, de-suburbanization, and anti-capitalism. In this panel, we hope to facilitate a conversation about art, in/convenience, precarity, and resistance in community. We also hope to consider alternate views of in/convenience: What can we do to create communities in which the inconvenience of slowness is celebrated rather than derided? How can we utilize writing to grieve futures that didn't materialize? How might we create work that celebrates the pleasure of systemic and interpersonal inconvenience? How can we build resilience to inconvenience and precarity at once, together? In the tradition of scholars and writers like Lauren Berlant, Hanif Abdurraqib, Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, and Margaret Price, how can we embrace the inconvenient as a site of connection and resistance? We welcome writers of creative nonfiction, poetry, fiction, art pieces, and hybrid works who seek to consider community and in/convenience. We are looking for writing about all forms of convenience and inconvenience, from the granular to the esoteric. After panelists share their work, the chairs will facilitate a conversation between writers and audience members.

Convention Site: Salve Regina University. Session Abtract The guiding thread of this panel develops around a curious remark by Jacques Rancière that would seem to amend a classically Aristotelian thesis: "man is a political animal because he is a literary animal," the fundamental condition of which is the "excess of words" constitutive of the human animal's politicalness. Literature (or poetry) has long been placed in close proximity to politics, as we find in Plato's Republic, where philosophy and literature-and, more generally, philosophy and politics-turn out to be perennial adversaries. That matters of literature bear upon the question of politics has featured in continental French thought for quite some time, considered in terms of the milieu of différance and event in Jacques Derrida; le partage du sensible and dissensus in Jacques Rancière; and the unpresentable and testimony to le différend in Jean-François Lyotard, among others. More recently, Geoffrey Bennington has taken up the question of the unreadable as that condition that keeps reading open to the event of alterity. What is at stake, then, in the complex relationship between literature and politics? How does literature bear witness to, or otherwise reconfigure, who counts as a speaking being, what is recognized as speech, and/or what falls out of discursive legibility as mere noise, excess, or silence? And how might mis-reading, mis-translation, and mis-understanding contribute to the politics of literature? This panel invites reflection on the figures, scenes, and events of textuality that respond to these and related questions. All critical approaches are welcome for this in-person panel. Eric J. Adamo McMaster University Hamilton, Ontario, Canada.

items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students' professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field's contributions. This roundtable invites faculty working in specialized institutional contexts to reflect on how they sustain and advocate for the Humanities amid these pressures. How do instructors articulate the intellectual, ethical, and professional value of Humanities study to students primarily focused on career-focused pathways? What pedagogical or curricular strategies have proven effective in demonstrating relevance to disciplines such as engineering, nursing, or business? Alternatively, how have faculty members built collaborations with colleagues across fields to integrate Humanities perspectives into specialized curricula? Participants will also consider how they engage multiple audiences-students, faculty peers, and administrators-to communicate the significance of Humanities education. By sharing concrete strategies, institutional experiences, and models of interdisciplinary partnership, this discussion aims to highlight adaptable approaches for maintaining the visibility and importance of the Humanities in specialized settings. Ultimately, the roundtable seeks to reassert the Humanities as essential to professional education. This roundtable is part of the Northeast Modern Language Association conference, which will take place between March 6-9, 2027 in Newport, RI. Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. 250-word abstracts for participation in this roundtable are welcome, and they can be submitted through this website: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/login

items.fullDescription: Palestine and the Challenge to German Studies Northeast Modern Language Association (NeMLA) annual convention Newport, Rhode Island March 6-9, 2027 Submission Deadline: 30 September 2026 through the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 Recent work in and around German Studies (Younes and Al-Taher; El Bulbeisi; Özyürek; Moses; Salehi) argues that the erasure of Palestinian identity in Germany is tied to deeper national tensions: How the country remembers its past, how it talks or avoids talking about race, what kinds of political speech are treated as acceptable, and how it confronts histories of imperialism and genocide. Moreover, scholars (Thompson and Tuzcu; Ragab; Daher) have documented how major institutions in Germany have been engaged in a wave of repression of ethnic minority communities, targeting Palestinians, other people of color, and Jewish anti-Zionists. This scholarship demonstrates how such pressures influence which voices, histories, and political positions are treated as legitimate within the field of German Studies, and which ones are marginalized. This panel invites contributions that explore how German Studies has begun or has struggled to engage with the significance of Palestine and Palestinian life, not only in contemporary German culture, politics, and literature, but within the discipline's own structures. While scholarship on Holocaust memory culture, as well as on multidirectional memory and migrant memory archives, has broadened the field's understanding of how Holocaust memory circulates and how migrant communities navigate its demands, recent work, such as articles by Catlin, Kundnani, and Rosenbrück in the New German Critique special issue "German Memory Politics at a Crossroads" (2026) provides evidence of the limits of these frameworks and the political pressures that shape them. Rather than challenge the centrality of Holocaust memory itself, this panel aims to examine how it is mobilized to foreclose other histories of violence, displacement, and coloniality, and how this foreclosing makes it difficult to integrate anti-imperialist, antiracist, and decolonial approaches that would situate Germany within broader histories of imperialism, colonial violence, and genocide. Palestine makes these dynamics visible by revealing how debates about memory shape disciplinary boundaries, how racialization and political speech determine scholarly legitimacy, and how exclusions are reproduced even within critical frameworks. This panel welcomes contributions that examine where Palestine appears, where it is actively excluded, and how these patterns expose German Studies' unresolved tensions around race, German colonial histories, and the politics of knowledge production. The goal of this panel is to open a conversation about how German Studies might expand beyond memory-centered approaches toward more globally attuned, anti?imperialist, and decolonial analytical frameworks. Topics include but are not limited to: · Intersectional decolonial feminist frameworks and praxes · Critiques of white Western imperial feminism · "Pinkwashing" and "homonationalism" to justify colonial violence and dehumanize Indigenous communities · The role of anti-Palestinian racism in mainstream anti-immigrant backlash and far-right political actors · Scapegoating of Muslims as the new Nazis in the theory of "imported anti-Semitism" (Özyürek) · Germany's colonial and neocolonial relationships to the broader region of West Asia · Integrating Palestinian perspectives into pedagogy, curriculum, and study abroad advising · Courses and lesson plans that include the Nakba and its continuity · German Studies and BDS/academic boycott · The "Historikerstreit 2.0" and attacks on "postcolonialism" · The history of East German solidarity with Palestinians · Student and faculty support in campus organizing for Palestine solidarity, and institutional and departmental barriers Abstracts: Please submit 300-word abstracts by 30 September 2026 though the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 For questions, please contact the panel organizer Maria Grewe (mgrewe@jjay.cuny.edu).

items.fullDescription: If you've taught older literature recently, you've probably heard students ask the question "Why am I reading this?" They've got a point. Why should we read Shakespeare's plays, or Paradise Lost , or (god-forbid) "The Rape of the Lock"? We might be able to coax students into reading a Jane Austen novel or even Huckleberry Finn because they are still part of our cultural imagination, but it's less easy to coax students into reading Beowulf or Tom Jones -texts that are less familiar in form and content. As we jettison the canon and the timeless truths of literature, what do we expect reading older texts will give our students that they wouldn't otherwise understand? How do we explain our reasoning to students about why they should read texts from earlier literary periods? How do we present these earlier periods (or periodization) and their culture and ideas as relevant to our undergraduate students in our English, writing, or humanities programs? Or is relevance the problem? How might we redefine older literature in our classes, or what we (can) do with these texts? I'm particularly interested in position papers that take into consideration practical pedagogical and theoretical concerns: arguments about curricula, course development or assignments that do different things with this literature. Papers are welcome on any kind of literature/texts or periods prior to 1800.

items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026.
