items.fullDescription: Digital Dirges: Video Games, Elegy, and the Rhetoric of Loss (McFarland, Studies in Gaming series) Editors: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University (mouellet@odu.edu) David Metzger, Old Dominion University (dmetzger@odu.edu) Project Overview: Video games are more likely to have a loss than a win condition. This means that players frequently confront a form that includes recursion, redemption, and repetition through a mode of elegiac literature. Thus, my panel will explore the interactive elegy offered by video games, both as a hermeneutic and a heuristic, which will be of use to literature scholars, creative writing instructors, and game designers alike. The current collection, then, explores the formal and thematic connections between the classical tradition of elegy-the discourse of mourning, loss, and remembrance-and the interactive medium of video games. Moving beyond traditional literary contexts, this volume argues that digital play actively constructs, mediates, and performs acts of mourning, remembrance (anamnesis), and fateful discovery (anagnorisis) essential to the elegy. Indeed, the classic arcade game, Missile Command, makes the player choose between protecting cities and defending missile bases. Its apocalyptic theme remains a common one as games have developed in terms of technologies and telling tales. Video games are, in fact, more likely to feature a loss than a win condition, meaning players frequently confront a form that includes recursion, redemption, and repetition through a distinctive mode of elegiac literature. As Classics scholar Michael Zimm (2019) argues, video games are now worthy of study based on their ability to produce compelling analogues of Greek literary forms. Indeed, in producing a literary narrative based on the reconciliation of mourning, masochism, and melancholia, video games comprise a previously unexplored area of elegiac literature. Beyond writing the lyrics of lament and loss, the player simultaneously interacts with and witnesses the dual literary processes of apotheosis (the attribution of divine or Christlike attributes, including releasing the divine through sacrifice) and anagnorisis (the literal "unignorancing" or moment of revelation of the means of dealing with the loss). Tellingly, video games, from Bioshock Infinite to Elder Scrolls to Red Dead Redemption, Gears of War, and Spec Ops games, to name just a few influential series, have taken up the traditional form of ritualized sacrifice and mourning. The act of losing, which is central to game design, is also a hallmark of elegiac prose (Regan 2017; Vickery 2009). The American elegy is a distinctive variant because of its emphasis on the one(s) left behind (Cavitch 2007), a precise entry point for games like The Last of Us, Dear Esther, and The Binding of Isaac. In games with strong allegories, like Dark Souls and Assassin's Creed, literal and figurative resurrection allows the game to combine quick apotheosis with the extended rhetorical work of anagnorisis, yielding a hybrid literary form. Thus, it remains to map and to theorize this emerging literary form. The peer-reviewed collection, Digital Dirges will explore the creation of the interactive elegy, both as hermeneutic and heuristic, since the player also participates in the literary process through an on-screen surrogate, adding yet another, unexplored, layer to the theorizing of an important literary form and its distinctive American literary variant. While the volume will contribute to Game Studies, it also offers a moment for the study of games to contribute to the understanding of established modes and forms. This exploration of the interactive elegy will be of use to literature scholars, creative writing instructors, and game designers alike. Topics may include but are not limited to discourses of gender in contexts of loss and the performance of mourning what games can teach us about narratives of mourning, and loss games, grief, melancholia, masochism and mourning the contradictory pleasures of losing individual, communal and national loss games as prose, poetic or hybrid elegy games, loss and apotheosis the loss of childhood and/or innocence in games being the one left behind and the "redemption arc" resurrection and recursion games and the American elegy the elegiac mode in specific games and series digital writing and/or rhetoric and elegy psychoanalysis and elegy environmental design as a tombstone, how non-player characters (NPCs) function as mourners the effects of proximity to or complicity in acts of loss. teaching the elegy with games We invite scholars from multiple disciplines to submit abstracts (300-500 words by 16 Oct. 2026 with completed papers due 15 March 2027. Please send abstracts and inquiries to the editors.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. items.fullDescription: Black Performing Arts: Sound, Movement, Image, Text Submission Deadline: October 31, 2026 The Black Performing Arts Area provides a scholarly forum to share research pertaining to Black performance across expressive forms. Broadly defined, the area focuses on all forms of performing and visual arts, including all musical genres, theatrical performance and performance art, performance elements in visual art, and connections between different Black expressive forms. In all these contexts we are interested in investigating where aesthetic technique and embodiment merge across Black diasporic expressivity. The panels on Black Performing Arts: Sound, Movement, Image, Text will showcase interdisciplinary discussions of cultural identity, art, religion, ritual, power, image, representation, symbols and their meaning, and the social processes and systems that influence and inform the innovation, production, regulation, and consumption of Black performing arts. Additionally, we invite research that examines the role of Black music within society, how Black performing and visual arts might be read intersectionally with attention to race, class, gender, and sexual identity, and the relationship between Black performing arts and their broad political and economic context. For the 2027 conference, we are particularly interested in research that explores the rich history of Black performance in Boston and New England, and for papers that connect to the conference's broad theme, "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture." Submissions must be made at https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Inquiries may be made to the Black Performing Arts area chair: Michael Borshuk Professor, Texas Tech University michael.borshuk@ttu.edu

items.fullDescription: The Mystery & Detective Fiction Area of the Popular Culture Association invites proposals for the annual conference in Boston, Massachusetts, March 24-27, 2027, to be held at the Boston Marriott Copley Place (110 Huntington Ave., Boston, MA). The deadline for submission is October 31, 2026. This year's PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Mystery & Detective Fiction are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We seek proposals from researchers, academics, graduate students, and independent scholars for scholarly discussions on all aspects and periods of mystery and detective fiction. Interdisciplinary approaches are strongly encouraged. We ask that proposals extend existing scholarship in new directions and avoid plot summary or review. Proposals should have a clear and focused argument that can be developed adequately in a 15-minute presentation. For the 2027 conference we are actively looking for submissions that would work as joint panels with the True Crime Area. We encourage topics that explore the mutual influence and exchange between True Crime and Mystery/Detective Fiction. You may indicate in your proposal if you would like your paper to be considered for a joint panel; even if not accepted for a joint panel, your abstract will be considered for our regular Mystery and Detective Fiction programming. Some possible topics for the 2027 conference: ? Boston-area mystery/detective/crime fiction/TV series/films-such as novels by George V. Higgins, Robert B. Parker, Hank Phillippi Ryan, Dennis Lehane; TV shows like City on a Hill, Spenser for Hire; films like The Departed, Mystic River, etc. ? Fiction re-imagining real-life crime events in Boston/nearby area, such as novels/film/TV about Fall River's Lizzie Borden, Boston's Whitey Bulger, etc. ? Subgenres, such as hardboiled detective fiction, eco-detective fiction, neo-noir, etc. ? The role of AI in detective/mystery fiction as theme or character ? Depictions of older characters as detectives or criminals ? Generic hybridity-detective/mystery crossed with horror, sci-fi, romance, dystopia ? Authors or texts featuring characters identifying with marginalized or historically excluded communities and their literary, social or political impact within the genre ? Transnational and global crime fiction ? Analysis of specific authors and/or time periods, including relevant tropes ? Adaptation of mystery and detective fiction in film, television, theatre, computer games, etc. Submission Process Please submit your 250-300 word abstract through the PCA conference's submission portal. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. If you are a first-time presenter in our area, please identify yourself with a note after your abstract: First-time presenters in Mystery & Detective Fiction are eligible for the Earl Bargainnier Award. To propose a panel, please submit individual presentations, then email the area chair with a request to be considered as a panel. The PCA/ACA requires a minimum of four papers per panel. In your email, name all participants and briefly explain the thematic link between your papers. About Us: The Mystery & Detective Fiction Area of PCA/ACA is dedicated to recognizing and promoting the scholarly study of all aspects of mystery and detective fiction, and to fostering an inclusive community for early-career scholars, adjuncts, grad students, and independent scholars, as well as established academics. Each year we also sponsor the George N. Dove Award for outstanding contributions to the serious study of crime fiction. We invite members and presenters to participate in our annual group dinner at the national conference and to join us at the annual business meeting, where we set the area's course for the next year. Finally, please send all inquiries to Marla Harris (mhcrocombe@gmail.com).

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: PCA Annual Conference, March 24-27, 2027: Boston, Massachusetts The Collecting and Collectibles Area invites proposals exploring how "collecting" has become an embodiment of the economic, political, environmental, and digital precarities that shape contemporary popular culture. Collecting now operates as a dynamic source for epistemic production, constantly redefining how popular culture is constructed, construed, mediated, valorized, historicized, and even contested. The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Collecting and Collectibles Area are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We welcome contributions that integrate practice-based, collaborative, comparative, transnational and cross-cultural approaches and involve innovative methods, community engagement, public and digital humanities to address topics including, but not limited to: --Emerging Technologies of Collecting: AI and collecting cultures, virtual archives, NFTs and blockchain collectibles, social media collecting communities, online marketplaces and economies, smart museums, mixed- reality collections, and AI-enabled smart twins of museums --Participatory Collecting Culture: Gaming memorabilia and sports collections, comic books, manga, anime, and graphic novels, fan archives, and exclusive/ limited editions --Popular Media collecting: Film and television memorabilia, music and vinyl records, cassettes, CDs, concert and artist-branded merchandise, celebrity memorabilia, fast-food promotional premiums, licensed toys, action figure and doll sets, LEGO, and theme park merchandise -- Heritage and Transcultural collecting: counter archives and collectibles, indigenous collections, digitality and heritage preservation, migration and portable collectibles, cultural diplomacy collections -- Crisis Collecting: Climate change and at-risk collections, pandemic collecting, trauma and collecting, sustainable and ethical colleting, resilient collections, commemorative coins and medals, satirical magazines, post-collapse souvenirs, war memorabilia -- Consumer Culture and Collecting: Auctions and collector markets and communities, investment collecting, branding and nostalgic collecting, resale platforms -- Materiality of Collecting: household collectibles, stamps, travel souvenirs, and their digital adaptations We welcome individual papers, complete panels, creative presentations, and interdisciplinary collaborations. Scholars, independent researchers, graduate students, and undergraduate students are encouraged to submit. Membership in the PCA is needed to submit a proposal. Submit a title and 150-200 word abstract through the PCA submission system. https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Presentations are typically 15-20 minutes. For complete panels, each participant should submit individually. For questions, please contact the Area Chair: Majda R. items.fullDescription: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years since these texts appeared, not the least of which was a Gothic-infused global pandemic and the insidious rise of artificial intelligence in daily life. Academics today are and have been teaching the Gothic at a time when the world's problems - rising fascism, global conflict, climate change, the devaluation of Higher Education, among many others - make the world itself seem downright Gothic. This collection will seek to provide updated reflections, evaluations, and strategies on teaching the Gothic and utilising or creating Gothic pedagogy in the contemporary moment and beyond. Courses on or including the Gothic are taught in a wide variety of venues within and outside academia; settings include community colleges, traditional undergraduate programmes, graduate programmes, community centres, prisons and reformatories. Classrooms themselves vary greatly, from giant lecture halls to small upper-level seminars to fully online virtual spaces. Students of the Gothic come from all ages and backgrounds, and include native speakers of English and students acquiring English later in life. These contexts, venues, and audiences present different challenges for the instructor, and require unique approaches to make for successful learning experiences. We are seeking contributions from a range of scholars at different ranks and types of institutions (as well as outside of them) to present a broad understanding of the diversity of how we study and teach the Gothic today, and to provide new directions for the future. We already have interest from an academic press. Potential topics might include but are not restricted to one or a mixture of the following: Teaching the Gothic in the midst of a crisis (e.g. pandemic, war, from a distance or physically within such spaces) Teaching the Gothic outside of the university / in non-traditional settings Challenges of AI to teaching the Gothic The use of various digital platforms in teaching / student research Gothic and the archives in contemporary times What texts (and which editions) absolutely must be on any Gothic syllabus (and why)? Gothic forms (teaching beyond traditional formats, for instance) Gothic theory as pedagogy (in times of crisis particularly) Syllabus organizational strategies and rationales: Chronological? Thematic? Canon? Decolonizing the Gothic syllabus Preparing for and managing class discussions about violence, sexual violence, trauma, discrimination, or other tough topics that arise in the Gothic? Strategies for teaching a Gothic course for an audience unfamiliar with the Gothic / unfamiliar with academia / non-traditional students. Gothic and public engagement / school outreach Opportunities for service learning / personal and professional development in the Gothic course Creative forms of assessment in the Gothic classroom Neurodivergence and the Gothic Designing assignments with AI in mind Cancel culture and the Gothic Co-editors Bridget Marshall (University of Massachusetts, Lowell) and Jen Baker (University of Warwick, UK) seek abstracts of 300-500 words for chapters which will demonstrate innovative approaches to teaching the Gothic or engaging with or creating new Gothic pedagogies, particularly situated within recent contexts. We are open to a variety of forms, including case studies, reflective essays, theoretically informed essays, and other formats that can best showcase pedagogical insights. If your proposed essay includes samples of work by students/participants we will require written permissions before publication. Please also include a brief professional bio of 300 words (max) with your abstract. Please send your abstract and bio by 10 November 2026 to Bridget_Marshall@uml.edu and J.Baker.5@warwick.ac.uk We are happy to answer questions at the same address.

items.fullDescription: About the Series Dramatis Personae is an annual cycle of interdisciplinary, outreach-oriented conferences dedicated to exploring theatre through the lenses and tools of the human and social sciences. Each edition takes a specific theme as a point of convergence for researchers from different fields (anthropology, sociology, psychology, education, philosophy, political science, organisational studies and other fields of the human sciences), inviting them to approach theatre not merely as the exclusive object of theatre studies, but as a privileged site where the great questions of human experience become visible, are tested, and are transformed. Dramatis Personae is born from the collaboration between Officine Teatrali, a centre for theatre research and studies, WakeUp, association for social promotion, and Antropolis, a cultural association for scientific outreach. Thanks to the sponsorship of the Municipality of Vanzago, this annual event takes place in the splendid setting of the Sala degli Affreschi at Palazzo Calderara. Theme of the First Edition There is a kind of knowledge that does not pass through words. It is transmitted through gesture, learned through imitation and contact, deposited in muscle, in breath, in the posture one assumes before another. It is the knowledge theatre has always carried, and which the human sciences have come to recognise as one of the fundamental ways in which human beings inhabit the world and hand it down. The first edition of Dramatis Personae chooses this borderland as its theme: bodies that know. Bodies that act, that teach without teaching, that carry within them collective memories and invisible competences. Bodies of actors who build stage presence through a training that is also a transformation of the self. Bodies that cross ritual thresholds, bodies that suffer and resist, bodies that work, that care, that lead. Thematic Areas Proposals are invited that engage with one or more of the following areas, each of which takes the stage as its point of observation and opens onto dialogue with one or more disciplines of the human and social sciences. 1. The Stage as a Laboratory of Embodied Knowledge Body techniques, habitus, tacit knowledge: stage presence as a form of knowledge that resists verbal transcription. 2. Theatre and Ritual: Bodies Crossing Thresholds Continuities and ruptures between ritual and theatrical forms, liminality, technologies of the collective body. 3. The Body on Stage as a Site of Power Bodily normativity on stage and beyond it: gender, disability, migration, exclusion and resistance. 4. The Stage as Pedagogical and Transformative Practice Theatre as an instrument of formation: of the actor, of the spectator, of communities. 5. Bodies on Stage that Testify and Resist Documentary theatre, theatre of memory, theatre of war: the body as witness. 6. The Performer's Body in the Digital Age Presence, liveness and technological mediation: what happens to the body when the stage becomes dematerialised. 7. The Body that Works, the Body that Cares, the Body that Leads The transfer of the performer's embodied competences into organisational, clinical and educational contexts. Proposals that, while not falling precisely within one of these areas, engage originally with the general theme of the edition are equally welcome. Submission Guidelines Contributions may be submitted by researchers (doctoral candidates, postdoctoral fellows, faculty members, independent scholars) in the human and social sciences, and by theatre professionals with a reflective disposition toward their own practice. Proposals must include: title of the contribution abstract (maximum 400 words), specifying the theoretical framework, method, and relevance to the theme of the edition a maximum of 5 keywordsa brief biographical note for the author(s) (maximum 150 words), with institutional affiliation, if any indication of the relevant thematic area (one or more of those listed above) Proposals may be submitted in Italian or in English. Conference presentations will last 15 minutes, followed by discussion. Selection Process Proposals will undergo an anonymous peer review process, conducted by a joint scientific committee composed of scholars from theatre studies and the human and social sciences. Between a minimum of four and a maximum of eight contributions will be selected, forming the presentations of the conference day, possibly distributed across two sessions. Deadlines Phase Date Deadline for submission of proposals: 30 october 2026 Notification of selection results: 30 november 2026 Submission of final texts for publication: 11 jenuary 2026 Conference day: 6 february 2027 Publication Contributions selected and presented at the conference will be considered for scientific publication in a dedicated volume, subject to a further peer review process on the complete texts. Programme Structure The event takes place at Palazzo Calderara and opens with a performance, serving as an introduction to this year's theme. This is followed by selected academic presentations, organized into one or two sessions. The afternoon is dedicated to hands-on workshops and concludes with a group reflection session. items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Volume 37, Issue 1 & 2 (2027) Dear Colleagues, Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies - Dil, Edebiyat ve Kültür Ara?t?rmalar? Dergisi, the official publication of the Department of Western Languages and Literatures at Istanbul University, invites submissions for its 2026 issues (Volume 36, Issues 1 & 2). An open-access, peer-reviewed, and multilingual journal published twice a year (June & December), Litera is indexed in ELSEVIER SCOPUS, Web of Science ESCI, MLA International Bibliography, DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals), ERIH PLUS, EBSCO Communication Source, EBSCO Central & Eastern European Academic Source, Gale Cengage and Ulrichsweb. While our core focus remains on literary studies, linguistics, and cultural studies, we welcome interdisciplinary approaches that combine literary and linguistic analysis with insights from cultural theory and media studies-provided they maintain a clear relevance to our aim and scope We welcome original research articles that engage with current debates and critical issues in the study of Western (American, English, French, Belgian, German, Swiss, Austrian, Italian, Spanish, Latin American and Modern Greek) languages, literatures, and cultures. Languages of Publication: English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish No processing or publication fees. Eligibility: Submissions are accepted from authors who hold a PhD. items.fullDescription: The International Journal of English Literature, Social Sciences, and Multidisciplinary Studies (IJELS) publishes original research papers, review articles, and case studies that advance scholarly knowledge across English literature, social sciences, and multidisciplinary studies. The journal provides a global platform for researchers, educators, and professionals to share innovative ideas, critical analyses, and interdisciplinary perspectives. Submission open to Current Issue Feedback Notification: within 1 Month after submission (Online Peer Review System) IJELS welcomes high-quality submissions on a broad range of topics, including but not limited to: English Literature and Language Studies - English literature, world literature, comparative literature, interdisciplinary approaches to literature, literature and media, critical theory, English language teaching and learning, communicative language teaching (CLT), task-based language teaching (TBLT), second language acquisition, English language testing and assessment, syllabus design and curriculum development, applied linguistics, corpus linguistics, discourse analysis, translation studies, English globalization, and English-speaking cultures. Social Sciences and Humanities - Anthropology, Sociology, Psychology, Political Science, Economics, Education, Geography, History, Law, International Relations, Criminology, Public Administration, Development Studies, Human Rights, Social Welfare, Gender Studies, and Ethics. Arts and Cultural Studies - Performing Arts (music, theatre, and dance), Visual Arts, Cultural and Cross-Cultural Studies, Media Studies, Communication Studies, and Philosophy. Business, Law, and Information Studies - Business Studies, Corporate Governance, Industrial Relations, Information Science, Library Science, and Paralegal Studies. Multidisciplinary Studies - Research that bridges multiple academic disciplines to address complex social, cultural, linguistic, educational, technological, or global challenges. IJELS particularly values cross-cutting studies that integrate methodologies and perspectives from different fields to generate new insights and foster innovation. IJELS encourages diverse theoretical, empirical, and methodological approaches that promote intellectual exchange and interdisciplinary collaboration, fostering research at the dynamic intersection of literature, language, social sciences, and multidisciplinary inquiry. Fundada en 1989, la Red de Investigación de Aprendizaje se reúne en torno a un interés común por el aprendizaje ?en sus vertientes tanto formal como informal? abarcando todos sus niveles: desde el aprendizaje durante la primera infancia, pasando por el periodo escolar, enseñanza secundaria y universitaria, hasta la educación para adultos que se desarrolla en las diferentes poblaciones y ámbitos laborales.
